 Μake us preferred on Google Tax refunds, account updates on popular streaming platforms, undelivered parcels, even a supposed inheritance: fraudsters keep finding new ways to deceive, persuade and profit. Each year, millions of euros vanish from the pockets of unsuspecting victims, and cyber fraud now ranks among the biggest threats facing individuals, organizations and businesses alike. Georgios Germanos, a Police Captain with the Hellenic Police Cybercrime Division, spoke to Ta Nea about the scammers’ endless creativity and nerve, why users miss the traps, and how to stay safe. “The most common cases we see involve phishing, a kind of digital data fishing in which the attacker tries to get us to click a link and enter our personal information,” Germanos explains. “The pretext changes daily, depending on the news. One day it’s a text about a traffic fine. The next, it’s a message about a delayed package that requires a customs fee before delivery.” Many classic scams also mix phone calls with online tactics, he adds. A caller poses as an employee of a trusted entity, such as a bank or an organization, and asks the victim to enter codes or transfer money. NEWSLETTER TABLE TALK

The most frequently reported cases include: 1. Crypto investment scams. Victims are urged to invest in nonexistent opportunities, set up digital wallets and make fraudulent transactions through them.
 2. Wallet breaches. Existing digital wallets are hacked to steal cryptocurrency.
 3. Romance scams. Usually run on social media, these involve “lovestruck” fraudsters asking for large sums they supposedly need.
 4. Phone scams. Callers pose as accountants, doctors, staff from HEDNO (Greece’s electricity distribution operator) and others.
 5. Phishing and smishing (SMS phishing). This is the most widespread method, with criminals impersonating legitimate companies or public services.
 6. Deepfake scams. These are among the most dangerous, because victims often cannot believe that what they see or hear is fake. Scammers use AI-generated audio and video to forge the faces and voices of people the public knows well. Even large companies get caught. “Criminals often use hacking techniques to step into the communication between companies, and when a payment is due, they ask for the money to be sent somewhere else,” Germanos says. “A business thinks it is paying a supplier in China for raw materials, but the money actually goes to the attackers’ own accounts in an unrelated country. We’ve had many such cases here in Greece, and companies have lost hundreds of thousands of euros, if not millions.” A case in point is the major cyberattack on well-known websites worldwide, which put the data of millions of users at risk. Zoom, CNN and IKEA were among the targets, and the attackers went after cryptocurrency, credit card details and cookies. The Cybercrime Division handles thousands of cases every year. How to protect yourself “The key is to understand that nobody gives away money online,” Germanos says. “People shouldn’t be easily convinced that they can make easy money on the internet.” His advice: • Be careful what information you enter. Phishing is now part of daily life, and fraudulent messages arrive every day. Don’t click on links.
 • Install antivirus software on the phones and tablets you use to check email.
 • Guard your card and online banking credentials. Only use official websites.
 • Use common sense. Don’t take online videos at face value. Even if the Finance Minister himself appears to be promoting an investment product, double-check it. “It takes critical thinking, and we shouldn’t assume that what we see online is real,” he concludes. Is there a typical victim profile? Not anymore, Germanos says. “Young and old fall for it, whether they’re internet-savvy or not. Even the most experienced users can be fooled. In recent years, AI has made it very easy for criminals to show up with fake identities, complete with photos, videos and voices, which makes them far more convincing. Today, anyone can be scammed.” cybersecurity
